name: Kira Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the finish carpenters on building sites, fitting doors, skirting and stair rails after the rough work is done. The trade certificate got me started; thirty years of checking the grain and the level made me good at it. I like handing a room over with doors that close cleanly, though carrying materials up stairs is wearing at fifty-eight. My partner and I have grown children, lower pay than other senior carpenters, and less than a month of expenses put away; there are few similar jobs close to home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a computer can speed an invoice, but it cannot hang a door straight. I would still make the foreman check the timber list before we waste a day waiting for hinges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A minor office change does not threaten my craft. The worry already here is low pay and a thin reserve, because one delayed contract could cost us the money we expected to put toward retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my finish-carpentry shifts and check the delivery list with the foreman before each job. In the first year I would ask my partner to set aside part of each paid overtime day, if those days come, so a late invoice does not empty the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the next gap between sites, even with AI barely changing anything. A neat invoice is no comfort when the work is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you set aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One quarter of an overtime day’s pay would be manageable, but only when the overtime is actually paid. Ordinary weekly pay goes to bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when a delivery is short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I send the apprentice back with the list and call the foreman before cutting anything. We can make a missing hinge visible without sacrificing a day’s wages.

say: **AI invoices** may help the office without replacing finish carpentry.
The **timber list** still needs a person to check it before work starts.
think: Our **low wages** and tiny reserve are worries even if technology changes little.
A delayed **site contract** could take money needed for retirement.
do: **Keep** fitting doors and checking each delivery list with the foreman.
**Save** one quarter of paid overtime earnings when overtime arrives.
S0.quote: A neat invoice is no comfort when the work is late.
fieldNote: Her **baseline risk** is intermittent site work and a reserve below one month of expenses.
She would **save new overtime pay**, not relabel money already held.

steps.text: Keep finish-carpentry shifts and check site deliveries
Save one quarter of paid overtime earnings when available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the foreman that faster buying and scheduling should leave enough time to fit stairs safely. A programme made in an office must still allow for an uneven wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the contractor uses AI planning to squeeze more rooms into each week, my gang could lose paid days when we cannot meet the schedule. I have few local employers to turn to and no savings for an expensive course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would note the fitting time and defects on each floor, then show those records to the foreman before accepting a shorter schedule. In the first year I would keep the gang working and apply for a posted local finish-carpentry opening only if the listed hours and wage cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a schedule that looks perfect on a screen and leaves our pay short. I do not mind honest competition; I mind being charged for a wall that was crooked before I arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which defect would you record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An opening out of square by a finger’s width means extra packing before a door can hang. I would date the photograph and note the extra hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another employer worth applying to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A vacancy I can actually travel to, with hours and pay written down. Our bills will not be covered by a promise of plenty of work later.

say: **AI schedules** must leave time to fit doors and stairs safely.
A **crooked wall** makes the office estimate unreliable.
think: Shorter **paid days** would hurt our household quickly.
Few **local employers** make changing jobs difficult when our savings cannot bridge a gap.
do: **Record** fitting times and defects for the foreman.
**Keep** the gang working while checking posted local vacancies.
**Apply** only where listed hours and pay cover household bills.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours from unrealistic schedules.
S1.quote: Our bills will not be covered by a promise of plenty of work later.
fieldNote: She uses **site records** before challenging a schedule, despite reluctance toward new tools.
A **job application** requires a posted nearby opening at workable hours and pay.

steps.text: Keep finish-carpentry gang working while recording defects
Apply for posted local carpentry job if listed hours and pay cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that AGI may handle drawings and orders by 2028, while robots that can fit doors like people are still about three years away. The contractor should not call a machine safe before it has been tested on a real site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still have hands-on work for a while, but a 2031 site robot could take the wages my partner and I need. With under a month saved, retirement is not a quick way out of the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the contractor for a written safety rule and a real, funded course place on robot inspection with paid time. If it is offered, I would take the course; in the first year after 2028 I would keep fitting doors and apply for a posted local inspection role only if its hours and pay meet our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the three-year gap, because it sounds longer than three rounds of bills but it is not. I would rather keep earning than gamble on an unpaid certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the safety rule cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A carpenter must check that a robot has fixed a frame and kept the escape path clear before the room is signed off. The person on site must have authority to stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no training place opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep doing paid carpentry and ask the contractor again for dates and funding. I will not take money from our small reserve for a course that has no local opening.

say: **2028 AGI** changes plans before capable site robots arrive around 2031.
Machine work needs **site inspection** and human stop authority.
think: A **2031 robot** could end wages I still need.
Less than **one month saved** makes immediate retirement unaffordable.
do: **Ask** for written robot safety rules and paid funded training.
**Take** an actual funded inspection course place if paid time is provided.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work only at bill-covering hours and pay.
feel: **Anxious** about losing needed wages before retirement is affordable.
S2.quote: I would rather keep earning than gamble on an unpaid certificate.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** shows in demanding proof and safety authority before changing trade tasks.
The **course and application** both depend on real places, funded paid time and workable local wages.

steps.text: Keep paid finish-carpentry work after 2028 while available
Take funded robot inspection course if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local inspection role if hours and pay cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the 2031 date gives employers time to trial the equipment properly before robots arrive about 2034. The crew should see the safety checks with their own eyes before anyone changes the fitting hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me more wages, if the contracts keep coming, but it does not make a new career easy at my age. I might retire before a 2034 robot comes, yet only if our household figures say we can live without my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the carpentry work and ask my partner to review our yearly income, bills and likely retirement costs each winter. In the first year after 2031 I would take a funded, paid-time robot inspection course if a place actually opens, then apply for a posted local inspection job only if its wage and hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious, though the extra years let me see whether this is a real threat. I can plan around paid work; I cannot plan around a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We need to add up what stopping work would cost, including housing, food and repairs, then compare it with income we could actually count on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful robot trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should fit a door in an uneven opening and let a carpenter check the fixings before sign-off. A flawless showroom wall proves very little.

say: **2031 AGI** leaves time to test construction robots before around 2034.
A **real site trial** matters more than a showroom demonstration.
think: My **retirement timing** depends on household figures, not the robot calendar alone.
Extra years help only while **contracts** keep paying.
do: **Keep** carpentry shifts and review retirement costs with my partner annually.
**Take** a funded robot course if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work only with bill-covering pay and hours.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to check facts over a longer period.
S3.quote: I can plan around paid work; I cannot plan around a brochure.
fieldNote: She considers **retirement** only after comparing actual household costs and income.
A **trial** must test uneven walls and allow a carpenter to check fixings before sign-off.

steps.text: Keep carpentry shifts and review retirement affordability annually
Take funded robot inspection course if actual paid-time place opens
Apply after funded course for posted local inspection job if hours and pay cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger carpenters that a decade is time to teach sound work, not an excuse to stop checking it. AGI may change the drawings in 2036, and capable site robots follow about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I may have left the ladders, but I cannot promise that now with our small reserve. I might continue paid inspection or teaching if we still need the money; I would leave only when a real budget supports it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting and checking doors while I can, and review our household bills and likely retirement income with my partner each year. If I still need wages after 2036, I would take a funded safety course only with an actual paid-time place, then apply for a posted local inspection or apprentice-training role only if its pay and hours cover our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about how little we have saved, though the long date gives me time to get the sums right. I would like to retire with my partner, but wishing does not settle the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to check a door opening before cutting timber, and why the site must keep a safe way out. I would teach that beside the work, not from a machine brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the figures do support leaving site work before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then my partner and I could choose a date together after checking income and expenses. Until then I would keep paid work rather than claim we are ready.

say: **2036 AGI** changes drawings before capable site robots around 2039.
Apprentices should learn **physical checks** alongside any future equipment.
think: I may leave ladders before **2039**, but our reserve cannot guarantee it.
Any **retirement date** needs real household income and cost figures.
do: **Keep** paid carpentry and review retirement affordability yearly.
**Take** a funded safety course only if a paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local inspection or training work only at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about savings, with time to make a budget.
S4.quote: I would like to retire with my partner, but wishing does not settle the bills.
fieldNote: Her **long runway** gives time to check finances without assuming a fixed retirement age.
Continued **post-2036 work** depends on income need; any role change needs paid training and a workable local posting.

steps.text: Keep paid carpentry while reviewing retirement affordability yearly
Take funded safety course if actual paid-time place opens and wages remain needed
Apply for posted local inspection or training role if pay covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I need the pay from my hands for longer than three years if our savings stay thin. Paid training with an actual place, a safe site trial and a posted local role at enough pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I do not object to a younger carpenter learning a new tool. I object to calling a machine’s unsafe shortcut progress just because it is faster.

portrait: **Kira Petrov**, 58, leads finish carpentry on building sites and holds a vocational trade certificate.
She and her **partner** have grown children, low pay, less than a month saved and few nearby construction openings.
She avoids **AI tools** herself and insists on site proof before accepting software schedules or robots.
She is **anxious** even in a mild scenario because delayed jobs threaten the wages she needs.
A **funded course** and posted local inspection work might help, while retirement remains conditional on household costs and income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens the late-career carpentry wages she still needs when site robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A real **paid training place**, safe site trial and posted local inspection job at bill-covering pay would help her plan.
headlineQuote: I object to calling a machine’s unsafe shortcut progress just because it is faster.
